# How to use this script

This document is a recording script, not a student-facing handout. It is organized around the same video segments already referenced in `Exercise_01.qmd` (Introduction, Step 1 through Step 5), so each section below can be recorded on its own while sharing the exercise document and the Posit Cloud project on screen.

Every section contains a literal, word-for-word script in blockquotes, meant to be read (or closely paraphrased) directly to students as the camera rolls. Stage directions — what to click, what to have on screen, when to pause — are written in *italics* above the line(s) they apply to, and are not meant to be read aloud. Because students are expected to read the full exercise text on their own, the script keeps background and context brief.

Coding is not the point of this class, so the script treats code chunks differently depending on what students are actually asked to do with them. For chunks marked "code-fold" in the document — the collapsed, optional-to-read functions that build the maps and plots — the script gives only a brief three sentences: enough to say what the chunk produces, not how it works internally. For chunks students are actually told to copy and paste into their own Posit Cloud script, the narration stays practical and specific about what to copy, what to edit, and where to paste it. In both cases, and especially once a figure is on screen, the emphasis shifts to the data: what the plot or map shows, and what to look for when analyzing it, since that is the actual point of the exercise. Reference code blocks are included only for chunks students copy and paste themselves.

# Video: Introduction

*On screen: the top of `Exercise_01.qmd`, showing the title, Purpose section, and the Optional Reading callout.*

> Welcome to Exercise #1: Transportation Mode Share, Pedestrian Fatalities and Urban Street Design. In this exercise, you're going to work with two nationwide datasets: commuting, or "journey to work," mode share data from the Census Bureau, and pedestrian fatality records from the Fatality Analysis Reporting System, or FARS. You'll use these datasets to look at how people get to work, and where pedestrian fatalities occur, in one US county that you choose yourself. By the end of the exercise, you'll have built interactive maps, trend charts, and a hot spot analysis for your county, and you'll finish by proposing a real, practical street design improvement for one intersection or corridor where fatalities have clustered.
>
> This kind of evidence — mode share trends, safety hot spots — is exactly what planners, engineers, and advocates use to make the case for safer streets, better transit, and more walkable neighborhoods. So as you work through this, you're not just practicing with data, you're doing the same kind of analysis that shapes real transportation decisions.
>
> Before you start, there's an optional reading in the document called *Dangerous by Design*, from Smart Growth America. It uses these exact same datasets — FARS and the Census ACS — to rank states and metro areas by pedestrian fatality rate. It's not required, but it's a quick, useful preview of where this kind of analysis leads.
>
> One more thing up front: this class has no coding prerequisite, and you won't be asked to write code from scratch at any point. All the code you need is already written for you. Your job is to run it, and in a few specific places, make a small, clearly marked edit — mostly just swapping in the ID number for your chosen county. Let's get started.

# Video: Step 1 — Open Exercise #1 in Posit Cloud

*On screen: the course announcement with the Posit Cloud invitation link, then the Posit Cloud workspace, then the Files panel showing `Exercise_01.R`.*

> Start by logging into the course Posit Cloud workspace called "Sustainable Urban Transportation," using the invitation link from the week #1 announcement. Once you're in, open the Exercise #1 project. This will launch a full R session right in your browser — you don't need to install anything on your own computer.
>
> In the Files panel, in the lower right of the screen, you'll see a file called `Exercise_01.R`. Click on it to open it in the editor. This is the one script you'll use for the entire exercise — every piece of code you run and every edit you make happens in this file, from here through the end of Step 4.
>
> Again, no coding background is expected here. You'll never be asked to write code on your own. What you will do is select code, run it, and occasionally change one small value, like a county ID number, before running it again.

*On screen: the package-loading code chunk, already present at the top of `Exercise_01.R`.*

```r
# Activate R packages
library(dplyr) # data wrangling with pipe syntax
library(tidyverse) # data wrangling
library(sf) # simple features geometry data
library(plotly) # interactive plots
library(leaflet) # interactive maps
library(leaflet.extras) # additional leaflet controls, such as fullscreen and reset view buttons
library(leafsync) # synchronizes panning and zooming across multiple leaflet maps shown side by side
library(spatstat.geom) # defines the spatial point pattern objects used in spatial analysis
library(spatstat.explore) # calculates kernel density estimates and other exploratory spatial statistics
library(terra) # processes raster data, such as the pedestrian fatality density surface
library(classInt) # calculates class intervals (e.g., natural breaks) for shading maps

# Set default options for numerical display
options(scipen=999, digits = 2)

# Load project data
load("data/Exercise_01.RData")
```

> At the top of the script, you'll see a block of `library()` lines. Each of these turns on a package — a bundle of pre-built tools — that the rest of the exercise depends on. You don't need to memorize what each one does, but here's the short version. `dplyr` and `tidyverse` handle general data wrangling — filtering, grouping, summarizing — and you'll see their pipe symbol, the `%>%`, used constantly throughout the script to chain steps together. `sf` handles geographic data: the county, state, and division boundaries used in every map. `plotly` builds the interactive trend charts and box plots you'll see in Step 3, and `leaflet`, `leaflet.extras`, and `leafsync` build the interactive maps, add controls like fullscreen and reset buttons, and let multiple small maps pan and zoom together. The last four packages — `spatstat.geom`, `spatstat.explore`, `terra`, and `classInt` — don't get used until Step 4, when you build the pedestrian fatality hot spot map, so just note them for now.
>
> Select all of these lines and click Run at the top right of the source panel. It may take a minute or two the first time, and you'll probably see a bunch of messages scroll by in the Console — that's normal. As long as you don't see a message that starts with "Error," you're fine.
>
> The last two lines are just as important. `options(scipen=999, digits=2)` just tells R to display numbers in plain format instead of scientific notation, and to round to two digits, so what you see on screen stays readable. And `load("data/Exercise_01.RData")` is the one line doing the real work: it loads a single file containing every dataset you'll need for this entire exercise — mode share data, county boundaries, all of it — already downloaded, cleaned, and ready to go. You will never need to download or clean raw data yourself in this class.

# Video: Step 2 — Download the template and select a county

*On screen: the exercise PowerPoint template link, then the rendered `fig-popbycountymap` map.*

> Next, download the exercise PowerPoint template using the link in the document, and save it somewhere you can find it. You'll come back to this same file five times over the course of the exercise, adding one figure to one slide at each step.
>
> Now you need to pick your county. Scroll down to the interactive map below, which shows total population by county across the United States. For this exercise, choose a large, urban county in the contiguous United States — specifically, one with a population over 500,000. The reason for that population threshold is simple: a bigger county gives you enough commuters and enough recorded crashes to see real, meaningful patterns, rather than noise from a small sample. That matters, because you're going to be drawing conclusions that could, in principle, inform real transportation policy.
>
> Hover over any county on the map to see a pop-up with its name, its 2024 population, its population density, and — importantly — its GEOID. Write that GEOID down. It's a five-digit code: the first two digits are the state, and the last three are the county. For example, 17031 is Cook County, Illinois, which is the worked example used throughout this document.

*On screen: the rendered `fig-popbycountymap` map. The code behind it is collapsed behind a "Show the county population map code" toggle — no need to expand it.*

> That map is built behind the scenes with a color scale, some pop-up formatting, and a stack of map layers, all folded away under a "Show the code" toggle since the coding isn't the point here. What matters is what's on screen: every county in the country shaded from light to dark by 2024 population, with the darkest counties being the largest — hover over any county for its name, population, density, and GEOID, and use the layers control in the upper right to compare the standard basemap against the satellite view. Take a few minutes here to actually browse and settle on your county, since every figure for the rest of the exercise builds on that one choice.

# Video: Step 3 — Transportation mode share analysis

*On screen: the Step 3 introductory text, briefly.*

> This step looks at commute mode share — how people get to work — using data from the American Community Survey, table B08301. This is a Census Bureau survey that's been running continuously since 2005, and it's the standard nationwide source planners use to track commuting behavior. One thing worth knowing: the Census question only captures the mode a person used for *most* of their commute distance. So someone who walks a few blocks to catch a train is counted as a transit commuter, not a walker. Keep that in mind so you don't over-read small walk or bike percentages.

## The plotting functions

*On screen: skip past the `fx_plot_modeshare()` and `fx_plot_activetrans()` function definitions — they're shown for transparency behind a "Show the code" toggle, not something you need to read line by line.*

> These two hidden functions are what generate every mode share chart in this step: one produces the percentage-based trend line for four commute modes, and the other produces a simple count of walk commuters by year. Both can run on the whole country or on a single county depending on what you feed them, which is exactly what the next two figures do. You'll see them called, not written, from here on.

*On screen: `fig-modesharetrends`, then `fig-modesharetrendscook`, side by side.*

> Below, `fig-modesharetrends` calls both of those functions on the whole country, giving you the nationwide picture: mode share on the left, total walk commuters on the right. Look for which lines are rising and which are falling over the fifteen years, and whether the shape of the walk line on the right — actual commuter counts — tells the same story as the walk percentage on the left. Copy this figure, along with the box plot coming up next, into slide #1 of your presentation, and write a few sentences about the trends you see.
>
> Now scroll down to `fig-modesharetrendscook`. This is your template. You'll see one line of code: `custom_geoid <- "17031"`. That's Cook County, Illinois, shown here as a worked example. Copy this whole code chunk and paste it at the *end* of your own script — not in the middle, at the very end — and then change `"17031"` to the GEOID for the county you picked back in Step 2. Run it, and you'll get your own county's version of both charts. Copy those into slide #2, and write a few sentences comparing your county's pattern to the nationwide one: does your county's trend move in the same direction as the country as a whole, or does it stand apart, and by how much?
>
> One habit to build right now: every time you copy a new chunk of code from this document, paste it at the end of your script, not somewhere in the middle. That keeps your script running top to bottom without errors, and it's the single most common thing that trips students up if skipped.

## Interquartile range plot

*On screen: `fig-modeshareboxplot`. The code behind it is collapsed behind a "Show the box plot code" toggle.*

> This box plot shows the full national spread of each travel mode's share in 2024, not just the average. Skip the code — the document already explains how to read the box, whiskers, and outlier dots — and instead compare the four modes directly: notice how tightly walk and bike are compressed near zero compared to drive-alone, and which modes carry the most outlier counties pulled far from the pack. Copy this chart into slide #1 alongside the mode share trend figure.

## County mode share maps

*On screen: skip past the two hidden helper functions, straight to the four resulting maps — walk, bicycle, transit, and drive-alone.*

> These four maps are all built from two functions folded away behind a code toggle, one that splits each mode into five color groups and one that draws the actual map, so there's no need to open that code. What matters is what you see: each map colors every county in the country by that mode's share of commuters, using the same basemap, outlines, and layer controls from Step 2. Cycle through all four before you start comparing, since the real analysis happens once you can see them side by side.
>
> As you look at these four maps, ask yourself: which modes cluster in just a few regions, and which are spread evenly across the whole country? Go back to the county you selected and compare it to its neighbors — are they similar, or does your county stand out? Try switching to the satellite layer to see if something visible, like a street grid, a college campus, or a coastline, might explain what you're seeing. And for the very large number of counties where driving alone is nearly universal, think about what trade-offs — economic, environmental, health-related — come with having few practical alternatives.

# Video: Step 4 — Pedestrian fatalities

*On screen: the Step 4 introduction, briefly.*

> This step shifts from commuting to safety, using the Fatality Analysis Reporting System, or FARS. Unlike the ACS, which is a sample survey, FARS is a full census: it records every single crash on a US public road that results in a death within 30 days, and it's been maintained by NHTSA since 1975. This is the dataset planners and safety engineers actually use to identify the most dangerous streets and intersections and to prioritize Vision Zero investments.

## Downloading and filtering the data

*On screen: the FARS download code chunk.*

```r
state_fips   <- as.integer(substr(custom_geoid, 1, 2))
county_fips  <- as.integer(substr(custom_geoid, 3, 5))

crashes_fars <- read_csv(paste0(
  "https://crashviewer.nhtsa.dot.gov/crashviewer/CrashAPI/FARSData/GetFARSData?",
  "dataset=Accident&FromYear=2010&ToYear=2024&State=", state_fips,
  "&county=", county_fips, "&format=csv"
)) %>%
  filter(state == state_fips, county == county_fips)

ped_fatalities <- crashes_fars %>%
  filter(harm_evname == "Pedestrian") %>%
  filter(latitude > -90, latitude < 90, longitud > -180, longitud < 180,
         !latitude %in% c(77.7777, 88.8888, 99.9999),
         !longitud %in% c(-77.7777, -88.8888, -99.9999)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitudname", "latitudename"), crs = 4326)
```

> Copy this chunk into your script, right after the mode share code, and run it. Here's what it's doing. The first two lines split your county's GEOID back apart into a two-digit state code and a three-digit county code, since that's the format the FARS data system expects. The `read_csv()` call after that builds a live request to NHTSA's CrashViewer system and pulls down every fatal crash recorded in your county between 2010 and 2024, directly into R — you don't need to visit any website or download any file by hand.
>
> The last block, `ped_fatalities`, narrows that full crash table down to the pedestrian-involved ones, and also drops a handful of placeholder coordinate values — numbers like 77.7777 — that FARS uses to flag missing or bad GPS data, so those don't end up plotted somewhere in the ocean on your map. The very last step converts everything into a proper spatial points layer, which is what makes it possible to map in the sections coming up.

## Fatality trend plots

*On screen: skip past the hidden `fx_plot_pedfatalitytrend()` function, straight to the resulting two-panel `fig-pedfatalitytrend`.*

> This hidden function is doing the work behind the next figure — sorting every fatality into a category and matching its colors to the walk and bike colors from Step 3 — but it's tucked behind a code-fold toggle since you don't need to read it. What you do need to look at is the output: a stacked area chart showing fatalities by mode over time on the left, and a simple pedestrian-only trend line on the right. Watch how thick the pedestrian layer is relative to the whole stack, and whether that share is growing over time or just the raw numbers are.
>
> Copy the code chunk that calls this function into your script, right after your FARS download code, and run it — it uses the `crashes_fars` data you just downloaded, so it automatically builds the chart for your own county. Copy both panels into slide #3, and write a few sentences describing the trend: is the pedestrian line rising, falling, or flat overall, and are there specific years with a sharp jump or drop worth calling out?

## Four-period fatality maps

*On screen: skip past the hidden `fx_map_pedfatalityperiods()` function, straight to the resulting synced four-panel map.*

> Before jumping straight to a formal hot spot analysis, this next map just lets you look at where fatalities have occurred over time. Behind the scenes it splits your county's pedestrian fatalities into four four-year windows and lines up four small maps, one per period, all sharing the exact same zoomed-in view of your county, so there's no need to open that code. All four panels pan and zoom together, so dragging or zooming on any one of them lets you instantly compare the same location across every time period.
>
> Copy the chunk that runs this function into your script. As you look at the four panels, watch for locations where fatalities show up again and again across multiple periods — those recurring locations are your best candidates for the formal hot spot analysis that comes next.

## Hot spot density map

*On screen: skip past the hidden `fx_map_pedfatalityhotspot()` function, straight to the final density surface map.*

> This is the most technical piece of code in the whole exercise, which is exactly why it's the one most worth leaving folded away — it takes your county's individual fatality points and turns them into a smooth surface, so that overlapping points build up into visible hot spots instead of just showing scattered dots. If you want the full technical explanation of how that surface is calculated, there's a callout box right beneath this figure in the document. What matters for the exercise is the result on screen: warmer colors show tighter clustering of fatalities, not raw counts.
>
> Copy the chunk that runs this function into your script, and look for hot spots — clusters of orange or red — in your own county's map. One important caution to pass along here, straight from the document: color intensity shows relative clustering *within your own dataset*. It's useful for comparing locations inside your county, but it's not a fixed, universal risk threshold you can compare across different cities or datasets.
>
> Copy this map into slide #4 of your presentation, and describe what you see. Then use the satellite layer already built into the map, or Google Street View, to actually look at one of the hot spot locations you identified.

# Video: Step 5 — Urban street redesign recommendations

*On screen: a hot spot location from the student's own map, viewed in the satellite layer or in Google Street View.*

> This step has no code — it's about looking, not coding. Take one of the corridors or intersections you flagged in your hot spot map, and pull it up in satellite view or Google Street View. Look closely at the street design: how many lanes, how wide are they, is there a marked crosswalk, how far does a pedestrian have to walk to cross, is there any kind of bike infrastructure.
>
> Then ask yourself: what about this design creates risk for someone on foot? And what specific change would you recommend? Don't just say "make it safer" — name an actual intervention: narrower travel lanes, a raised crosswalk, a protected bike lane, a shorter crossing distance, a curb extension. If you're not sure what's realistic, the document points you to two resources: NACTO's *Urban Street Design Guide*, which catalogs specific treatments by street type and problem, and the Chicago Department of Transportation's *Pedestrian Program*, which shows how one real city applies this same hot-spot-driven approach in practice. Use slide #5 to show the location and summarize your recommendation.
